name: Mitanni
place: the Khabur river lands of northern Syria
desc: A Hurrian kingdom ruled by chariot lords whose kings bore Indo-Aryan names and swore by Mitra, Varuna and Indra. Their horse-trainers wrote the oldest horse manual, and their singers left the oldest written melody.
source: Amarna letters of King Tushratta; the Mitanni–Hittite treaty (c. 1380 BCE); the Nuzi archives; the capital Washukanni has never been firmly located

cautious: Keeper of the Tablets of Nuzi

belligerent: won a chariot and a pair of horses in the king's service
cautious: walked the horses through the river at dawn for a hundred days
devout: sang the hymn to Nikkal with the lyre tuned in the new way

inventions.name: Kikkuli's Horse Training
inventions.source: The Kikkuli text (c. 1400 BCE), written for the Hittites by a horse-trainer 'of the land of Mitanni': a 214-day programme
inventions.desc: Horses walked, trotted, swum and fed by the day for seven months: everyone travels 8% faster.
inventions.hint: Needs Beast Domestication, and long days of riding out.

inventions.name: Light Spoked Chariot
inventions.source: The maryannu, a chariot-owning warrior class, are named in Mitanni and Nuzi texts
inventions.desc: A light car on spoked wheels, quick enough to circle an enemy and shoot: +2 attack.
inventions.hint: Needs Beast Domestication and Polished Stone Tools.

inventions.name: Nuzi Ware
inventions.source: Fine cups painted white on a dark ground, typical of the Mitanni kingdom
inventions.desc: Tall cups painted with white birds and flowers on black: +2 mood, the stores hold 10 more food.

inventions.name: Written Melodies
inventions.source: Hurrian Hymn no. 6, to the goddess Nikkal, from Ugarit (c. 1400 BCE): the oldest substantially complete written music
inventions.desc: Songs for the lyre written down with the tuning and the notes: +3 mood, and a little more lore.
inventions.hint: Needs the Tribe & Agrarian Era, and songs at the rites and the fire.

foods.name: Lentil Pottage
foods.desc: Lentils and barley stewed thick with onions: hunger grows 10% slower.

foods.name: Raisin Cakes
foods.desc: Grapes dried in the sun and pressed into cakes: +2 mood, food spoils 5% slower.

finds.name: Wild Lentils
finds.desc: Low plants with flat seed pods, one of the first crops of the Fertile Crescent.

finds.name: Wild Vines
finds.desc: Vines climbing the trees at the forest edge, with small dark grapes.

people.name: Ehli-Teshup
people.desc: He knows each horse by its gait in the dark.
memory: caught a wild mare on the steppe and gentled her

people.name: Ashte
people.desc: Her songs are the tribe's memory.
memory: sang the old songs at three weddings in one moon

people.name: Tushratta
people.desc: A king of Mitanni whose letters to Pharaoh ask, again and again, for gold 'as plentiful as dust', and who sent the healing statue of Shaushka to Egypt.

people.name: Tadu-Heba
people.source: Amarna letters; she married Amenhotep III and perhaps later Akhenaten
people.desc: Tushratta's daughter, sent to Egypt with a long list of dowry gifts to seal a peace.

people.name: Tehip-tilla
people.source: The family archive of Tehip-tilla at Nuzi, 15th–14th century BCE
people.text: a wealthy man who has been 'adopted' by a dozen families, each time inheriting a field.
memory: was adopted by more fathers than any man in Nuzi
people.desc: A Nuzi landholder who got around the ban on selling family land by having the sellers adopt him.

people.name: Kikkuli
people.label: Kikkuli the Horse-Trainer
people.desc: A master of horses. Foraging 7, fast as a chariot.

people.name: Saushtatar
people.label: Saushtatar, who Plundered Ashur
people.desc: A chariot king who carries Ashur's silver doors home. Combat 8.

people.name: Ammiya
people.label: Ammiya, Singer for Nikkal
people.desc: Her songs are copied from Ugarit to Hattusa. Lore 7, mood of the whole tribe.

events.title: A Daughter for a Distant King
events.source: Mitanni princesses married Egyptian pharaohs to seal alliances; their dowry lists survive in the Amarna letters
events.text: A powerful neighbour asks for a bride from the chief's family, with a proper dowry, to bind our peoples together.

options.label: Send her with gifts
options.result: She leaves with a long train of gifts and a lyre. Raids from that side stop.

events.title: Adopt Me, and I Will Pay
events.source: Nuzi 'sale-adoption' contracts: family land could not be sold, so buyers were adopted as heirs
events.text: A rich stranger offers silver and grain to any family that will adopt him as a son and leave him a field. The old law forbids selling land, but says nothing about sons.

options.label: Adopt him
options.result: The family has a new 'son' older than the father, and a full granary.

options.label: Land stays in the family
options.result: The stranger goes to the next village to try again.

events.title: Send the Goddess to Heal Him
events.source: Tushratta sent the statue of Shaushka of Nineveh to Egypt when Amenhotep III was ill (Amarna letter EA 23)
events.text: A friendly chief far away has fallen sick. His people beg us to lend them our shrine's holy image, so that our goddess may heal him.

options.label: Lend the image
options.result: The goddess travels with an escort and comes home months later, with gifts. The chief lived.

options.label: She stays with us
options.result: The image stays in its place.

tales.name: Kingship in Heaven
tales.source: The Hurrian Kumarbi cycle, preserved in Hittite
tales.text: Alalu was king in heaven for nine years, until Anu threw him down. Anu ruled nine years, until Kumarbi bit him and swallowed his seed. From that seed, inside Kumarbi, grew the Storm God Teshub, who burst out and became king of the gods.
tales.moral: every reign gives way to the next

tales.name: The Bulls of the Storm God
tales.source: Hurrian religion: Teshub's bulls Sheri and Hurri, 'Day' and 'Night'
tales.text: Teshub's chariot is drawn by two bulls, Sheri and Hurri, Day and Night. When they run, thunder rolls. When the storm god wants to rest, the bulls graze on the mountains of Hazzi and Nanni, and the sky is clear.

tales.name: The Hymn to Nikkal
tales.source: Hurrian Hymn no. 6, Ugarit, c. 1400 BCE
tales.text: The singer tunes the nine-stringed lyre and sings to Nikkal, goddess of the orchards: a woman who could not bear a child brings her an offering of sesame oil, and asks. The words are partly lost, but the notes were written down, and three thousand years later they were played again.
tales.moral: a song can outlive its words

tales.name: The Gods of the Oath
tales.source: The Mitanni–Hittite treaty, c. 1380 BCE, invoking Mitra, Varuna, Indra and the Nasatyas
tales.text: When our kings swear, they call on the gods of their fathers, who came long ago from the far east: Mitra who keeps the oath, Varuna who sees every lie, Indra the warrior, and the twin horsemen. Whoever breaks the oath, these gods will hunt down.
